query: Traditional fusion welding can be unsuitable for repairing certain damaged high-value components because their physical and microstructural characteristics create a risk of hot cracking. For preventing or delaying surface-defect initiation, earlier work has used PVD, CVD, electroplating, and thermal diffusion to improve hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, but these approaches can involve costly deposition equipment, pollution, or long processing times. Under the constraints of avoiding whole-part replacement and limiting these drawbacks, what intervention could repair or improve the surface for service in aggressive environments? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to traditional fusion-welding repair and an untreated surface, its processing and service boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a laser cladding repair that deposits a Y and Hf co-doped high‐entropy alloy (EHEA) coating, optionally followed by shot peening, will create a surface with a refined multiphase microstructure and induced compressive residual stress. This composite repair will delay the initiation of hot cracking and reduce hot corrosion scale spallation compared to traditional fusion welding repairs and untreated surfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐value, damaged metallic component with surface defects and microstructural inhomogeneities that predispose it to hot cracking under high-temperature, corrosive conditions.
generation.intervention: Laser-directed energy deposition (laser cladding) of an EHEA coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) co-doped with Y and Hf, potentially followed by shot peening to induce beneficial compressive residual stresses.
generation.conditions: The processing should be performed using optimized laser cladding parameters that avoid additional thermal damage; post-deposition shot peening (if used) must be controlled to generate a uniform compressive stress field. In service, the component is exposed to high temperatures (around 900 °C) and aggressive environments (e.g., molten salt mixtures of Na2SO4 and NaCl) similar to those in hot corrosion tests.
generation.structural_mediator: A multi-phase microstructure comprising FCC, BCC/B2 phases, and an Al-rich L12 precipitate (developing after heat treatment) reinforced by compressive residual stresses from shot peening.
generation.mechanism: The deposition of a high-entropy alloy coating provides a refined, thermally stable microstructure that resists crack initiation. The co-doping with Y and Hf improves the adhesion and stability of the protective oxide scales, while any induced compressive residual stress from shot peening reduces tensile stress concentrations at the surface, delaying hot-cracking and mitigating spallation under corrosive conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The repaired surface should exhibit significantly reduced incidence of hot cracking and lower percentages of hot corrosion oxide scale spallation compared to surfaces repaired via traditional fusion welding and untreated substrates, with mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and hardness) approaching that of the base material.
generation.baseline: Performance of traditional fusion welding repair, which is prone to hot cracking, and the untreated component surface that lacks protective modifications.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this repair method is expected to be limited to scenarios where the damage is superficial and repairable via coating deposition; extreme geometries or extensive damage may not benefit equally. The performance improvements are also contingent on precise control of laser cladding and shot peening parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in thermal stability and corrosion resistance remains to be established, and trade-offs regarding coating ductility or residual stress distribution may arise. Further, the long-term behavior under cyclic thermal and chemical stresses is not yet fully documented.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of identical high-value metallic components: one repaired with traditional fusion welding, one with the proposed laser cladding (EHEA with Y and Hf co-doping) with optional shot peening, and one group left untreated. Subject all samples to post-repair heat treatment if applicable. Expose them to accelerated service conditions (900 °C under a corrosive environment of 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl molten salts) for a defined duration. Monitor microstructural evolution, measure residual stresses, and quantify hot corrosion spallation areas along with performing mechanical tests (tensile strength and hardness).
measurements: Percentage of surface area with oxide scale spallation (via image analysis or microscopy)
Phase identification and microstructure (by XRD and SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-cladded (and optionally shot-peened) repair does not show a statistically significant reduction in spallation area and incidence of hot cracking, or if its mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength) are not at least comparable to that of conventional fusion welding repairs and clearly superior to untreated specimens, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat

## Abstract
AbstractThe number of easily destroyed parts with high value is increasing in industry, and green remanufacture engineering is now mainstream in this new and expanding industrial field. Equal–additive–subtractive manufacturing, as a new technology that combines strengthening technology, additive manufacturing, and machining technology has great potential for development in the area of remanufacturing. Aiming at the damage characteristics of a plunger rod, this paper carries out a study about the repair technology by equal–additive–subtractive manufacturing of laser-directed energy deposition and shot peening. It was found that the microstructure of the materials repaired by equal–additive–subtractive technology is finer and the tensile strength can reach 100.4% of the base material. The surface residual stress of cladding materials changes from tensile stress to compressive stress, which reduces forming defects.
